food.text: From 8000 to 3500 BC, people on the Korean Peninsula lived mainly by hunting and gathering both land and sea resources. Archaeologists place this long stretch in the Mesolithic cultural stage, because true farming had not yet begun.

Pottery has been used on the Korean peninsula since prehistoric times for food storage. The origin of onggi, earthenware used as tableware and storage containers, dates to around 4000 to 5000 BCE. Onggi have been used continuously from then to the modern day.

Japan's Jōmon period, dated 14,000 to 300 BCE, was a time of semi-sedentary hunter-gatherer life. Archaeological studies of early Japanese Neolithic settlements reveal that seafood was of paramount importance from early times.

Korean archaeologists date the Neolithic to begin in 8000 BC, a label borrowed from Europe, where settled life, pottery and farming go together. Yet palaeoethnobotanical studies indicate the first bona fide cultivation did not begin until circa 3500 BC. The earliest known Korean pottery, Yunggimun pottery, dates to c. 8000 BC or before.

The people of the Jeulmun, whose comb-pattern pottery appears after 7000 BC, lived by a broad spectrum economy. They hunted, gathered and foraged, and also practiced small-scale cultivation of wild plants.

The word Jōmon was first applied to the pottery, and then to the whole culture, by the American Edward Sylvester Morse. The Jōmon people were nomadic hunter-gatherers who later practiced organized farming.

Comb-pattern pottery covering whole vessels is concentrated at sites in west-central Korea between 3500 and 2000 BC, when settlements such as Amsa-dong and Chitam-ni existed. It was during the Jeulmun that the cultivation of millet and rice was introduced to the Korean peninsula from the Asian continent.

Onggi, whose origin dates to around 4000 to 5000 BCE, includes patternless, mumun, and red-and-black earthenware. The patternless kind is made with lumps of clay and fine sand, while the red-and-black kind excludes any sand. The color is determined by the iron content of the clay and the method used to fire it.

Korean archaeologists propose a Neolithic beginning in 8000 BC, even though the first real cultivation did not begin until about 3500 BC. The period from 8000 to 3500 BC corresponds to a Mesolithic stage dominated by hunting and gathering. Pottery, in other words, appeared in Korea long before farming.

art.text: Jōmon pottery is said by many scholars to be the oldest yet discovered in the world. The culture takes its name from the "cord-markings", impressions made with rope, that decorate its pots. The term was first applied to the pottery, and then the culture, by American Edward Sylvester Morse.

The earliest known Korean pottery dates back to about 8000 BC or before. Known as Yunggimun pottery, it has been found across much of the Korean peninsula. Sites include Gosan-ri in Jeju Province and Ubong-ri in Greater Ulsan.
The earliest examples of Korean art are Stone Age works dating from 3000 BC. They mainly consist of votive sculptures and, more recently rediscovered, petroglyphs.

Jōmon communities numbered hundreds or even thousands of people. They lived in simple houses of wood and thatch set into shallow earthen pits, which drew warmth from the soil. Their crafts included lavishly decorated pottery storage vessels, clay figurines and crystal jewels.

The Jōmon people made clay figurines called dogū alongside their decorated pottery. These are among the crafts of a culture that began around 10,000 BCE and lasted until about 350 BCE. The Jōmon are generally said to have been the first settlers of Japan.

Comb-pattern pottery, called Jeulmun, appears in Korea after 7000 BC. Between 3500 and 2000 BC, vessels decorated with comb patterns over their whole surface concentrated at sites in west-central Korea, such as Amsa-dong and Chitam-ni.
The best preserved Korean pottery goes back to Paleolithic times around 10,000 BCE, according to one account. The same source places the start of the Neolithic period around 6000 BCE.

Jeulmun pottery shares basic design and form with pottery from far beyond Korea. Similarities are noted with the Russian Maritime Province, Mongolia, the Amur and Sungari River basins of Manchuria, and the Baiyue of southeastern China. It also resembles the Jōmon culture in Japan.

Early Korean societies depended mainly on fishing, and they used pottery to store fish and shellfish gathered from the sea. Pottery from the east coast tended to have a flat base, while pottery from the south coast had a round base. Korean pottery was recognized as early as 6000 BCE.

science.text: The Jōmon people of Japan are named for the "cord-markings", impressions made with rope, found as decorations on their pottery. Many scholars say Jōmon pottery is the oldest yet discovered in the world. The Jōmon period began around 10,000 BCE.

Some archaeologists suggest that raised-clay Yunggimun pottery from Gosan-ni on Jeju dates to 10,000 BC. If that is true, it would rank among the oldest known pottery in world prehistory, alongside finds from central and southern China, the Japanese archipelago and the Russian Far East.
The earliest known Korean pottery dates to about 8000 BC or before. Called Yunggimun pottery, it is found across much of the peninsula, at sites such as those in Jeju Province and Greater Ulsan.

Jeulmun means "Comb-patterned". Classic Jeulmun pottery, called Bitsalmunui, has comb-patterning, cord-wrapping and other decorations across the entire outer surface of the vessel. It appeared at the end of the Early Jeulmun period.

The Early Jeulmun period, about 6000 to 3500 BC, was marked by deep-sea fishing, hunting, and small semi-permanent settlements with pit-houses. Sites such as Seopohang, Amsa-dong and Osan-ri show this way of life.

Samples of the Gosan-ni pottery were radiocarbon dated. One result, 10,180±65 BP, supports a very early date, but other dates are somewhat later. The scholar Kuzmin suggests that more absolute dating is needed before the question can be settled.

Comb-pattern Jeulmun pottery, found in Korea after 7000 BC, has basic design and form similarities to pottery from the Russian Maritime Province, Mongolia, the Amur and Sungari River basins, and the Baiyue of southeastern China. It also resembles the pottery of the Jōmon culture in Japan.

According to a study by Schmidt and Seguchi, the prehistoric Jōmon people descended from Paleolithic populations of Siberia, in the area of the Altai Mountains. Other scholars note Jōmon similarities to Siberian populations, and there were likely multiple migrations into ancient Japan.

Radiocarbon evidence from shell-midden sites such as Ulsan Sejuk-ri, Dongsam-dong and Ga-do Island shows that shellfish were exploited. Many archaeologists nonetheless maintain that true shell middens did not appear until the later part of the Early Jeulmun period.

One study links certain Jōmon ancestry, the genetic lines C1a1 and C2, to "Tungusic-like people" who arrived from Northeast Asia in about 6,000 BC. They are said to have introduced the Incipient Jōmon culture, typified by early ceramics such as the Ōdai Yamamoto I Site.

culture.text: Around the Middle Jōmon period, clay figurines of people and animals called dogū appeared. They are often described as "goggle-eyed", with elaborate geometrical designs and short, stubby limbs. Scholars speculate they had religious significance and were used in fertility and healing rituals.

The Jeulmun pottery period of Korean prehistory is named for "Comb-patterned" pottery vessels, which form a large part of the pottery found consistently over the period, especially 4000-2000 BC. Its people lived by hunting, gathering, and small-scale cultivation of plants.

Palaeoethnobotanical studies indicate that the first bona fide cultivation in Korea did not begin until circa 3500 BC. The period from 8000 to 3500 BC therefore corresponds to a Mesolithic stage dominated by hunting and gathering of land and marine resources.

Yunggimun pottery, decorated with raised-clay patterns, appears at southern Korean sites such as Gosan-ni in Jeju Province and Ubong-ni in Ulsan. Some archaeologists suggest the Gosan-ni pottery dates to 10,000 BC. If so, it would be among the oldest known pottery in world prehistory.

The Early Jeulmun period (c. 6000-3500 BC) was characterized by deep-sea fishing, hunting, and small semi-permanent settlements with pit-houses. Examples include Seopohang, Amsa-dong, and Osan-ri. Shellfish were also gathered, as shown at coastal shellmidden sites such as Ulsan Sejuk-ri and Ga-do Island.
The oldest examples of Jōmon pottery have flat bottoms. Pointed bottoms, meant to be held in small pits in the earth like an amphora, became common later.

Jeulmun pottery bears design and form similarities to pottery of the Russian Maritime Province, Mongolia, the Amur and Sungari River basins of Manchuria, the Baiyue of southeastern China, and the Jōmon culture in Japan. Pottery with comb-patterns over the whole vessel is concentrated at sites in west-central Korea between 3500 and 2000 BC.

One study suggests that a "Altaic-like" population migrated from Northeast Asia to the Japanese archipelago in about 6,000 BC. It is linked to the Incipient Jōmon culture, typified by early ceramic cultures such as the Ōdai Yamamoto I Site.
